A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CDTD research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data experiments on six datasets, comparing four baselines and three CDTD noise-schedule variants in Section 4 and Appendix H.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on eleven datasets, component ablations, learned-schedule diagnostics, qualitative analyses and timing results in Section 4 and Appendices K–P.

M1.justification: V2 replaces v1's Diffusion Transformer with a TabDDPM-style MLP using five fully connected layers and 16-dimensional categorical embeddings. It adds learned time-dependent normalization of the joint loss and changes noise-schedule initialization from approximately uniform to emphasizing low noise levels, with mu changing from 0.5 to 0.25. These substantially revise the architecture and training procedure while retaining the joint Gaussian diffusion framework.

E1.justification: V2 retains all six original datasets and adds acsincome, covertype, diabetes, lending and news. This expands evaluation into additional income, forest-cover, hospital-readmission, lending and news settings, including high-cardinality categorical features. Appendix E specifies binary task conversions for covertype and diabetes.

E2.justification: The four evaluated baselines—ARF, CTGAN, TVAE and TabDDPM—are retained. CoDi, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator, including on the original datasets. Its results are omitted for diabetes and lending because of estimated training cost. STaSy and Diffusion Forest remain discussed rather than evaluated.

E3.justification: V1's 25-trial generator tuning with 10,000–20,000 training steps is replaced by fixed architectures calibrated to approximately three million parameters on adult and 30,000 training steps. V2 also changes diffusion sampling settings, increases detector tuning from 25 to 50 trials, introduces a 50,000-sample evaluation cap, revises downstream learners and metrics, and replaces signed DCR differences with absolute differences. Rank aggregation introduces explicit penalties for unavailable baseline results.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained comparison of three schedule granularities, v2 adds a five-configuration ablation across four datasets, testing grouped homogenization components, schedule functional form, type-specific schedules and initialization (Table 2 and Appendix O). Appendices K–M add learned-schedule fit diagnostics, univariate and bivariate distribution comparisons, and feature-level correlation-error visualizations.

E5.justification: Both versions already report five generation seeds and ten downstream-model seeds. V2's predictive-result captions explicitly incorporate these seeds into the uncertainty description, whereas v1 describes standard deviations across model averages. V2 also adds plus/minus quantities to average ranks. Some ambiguity remains because its captions mention four downstream models while Section 4.1 and Appendix I list three.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded with new datasets, CoDi, AUC, ablations and timing measurements. For example, adult CDTD per-type correlation error changes from 0.094 to 0.125 (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 7), under revised models and settings rather than a controlled performance comparison. V2 also resolves v1 Table 1's apparent JSD/Wasserstein label swap relative to its appendix averages.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix B adds an analytical derivation showing how output initialization yields expected unit loss across timesteps for both data types, extending v1's terminal-time calibration argument. Appendix A explicitly incorporates EDM weighting and preconditioning. Sections 2.1 and 3.3 correct diffusion coefficients to include the noise-schedule derivative. The existing logistic CDF, inverse and density derivations are retained in Appendix D.

C1.justification: The original claims about joint Gaussian diffusion and adaptive schedules remain. V2 broadens the central contribution to initialization and data-type homogenization, and makes scalability a prominent claim: faster training, improved handling of high-cardinality features and accommodation of arbitrary category counts. These extend the paper's claimed contribution beyond v1's emphasis on sample quality and competitive sampling speed.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for emphasizing low noise levels, slower convergence with feature-specific schedules, and TabDDPM's apparent preference for categorical fidelity. It discusses mixed effects in the component ablation and explicitly acknowledges ARF's categorical-marginal advantage. New limitations address schedule-selection cost, embedding-initialization sensitivity, privacy-sensitive applications and possible disadvantages on specialized data such as time series.

D1.justification: Appendices F–J substantially expand implementation information with baseline package versions and sources, licenses, RTX 4090 hardware, PyTorch 2.2.2, architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, EMA decay and warmup. Appendix P supplies detailed runtime measurements. However, v1's quantile-transformation and dequantization instructions disappear; this establishes lost documentation, not that preprocessing actually stopped.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of Diffusion Forest's scalability and cites Karras et al. (2023) and Kingma and Gao (2023) for adaptive loss normalization, alongside additional dataset and software references. References connecting v1 to non-uniform diffusion, Diffusion Transformers and numerical-feature embeddings disappear. The principal positioning around score interpolation and mixed-type diffusion remains intact.

P1.justification: The introduction, method explanation and discussion are extensively rewritten. V2 adds an explicit contribution list, reorganizes the method into framework, homogenization, noise schedules and customization subsections, and introduces a dedicated limitations section. The appendices are substantially reorganized while retaining and expanding earlier calibration and timewarping material.

P2.justification: The framework diagram is redrawn, and v2 adds architecture, noise-schedule, runtime, density and correlation-heatmap figures. The main results table changes from mean metric values to ranks, with updated mean results in Appendix N. Detailed tables gain comparator and real-data columns, while new ablation and runtime tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for its design choices through component ablations, broader benchmarks, explicit architecture and training-budget controls, and an initialization derivation. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility, and the JSD/Wasserstein summary inconsistency is corrected. Fixed baseline configurations replace per-dataset tuning, preprocessing documentation is lost, and learner-count captions remain inconsistent. Nevertheless, the gains in experimental scrutiny, mathematical explanation and transparency are substantial; the judgment does not depend on treating revised scores as performance gains.
